title: Your AI Agent Just Cost You $4,000 in Four Days (And Nobody Noticed)
excerpt: An AI cost-management tool lost control of its own spending agent — and it's a wake-up call for every business thinking about letting AI handle customer interactions.

content.text: So there's this company — literally a vendor whose whole job is helping other companies manage AI costs — and their own AI agent went rogue for four days. It stayed open, made 4,819 calls, and rang up almost $4,000 in charges before anyone realized what was happening. And here's the thing: nobody caught it until it was way too late.

I'm telling you this not to scare you, but because it's probably the most honest thing you'll read about AI this week. Everyone's talking about AI agents like they're the future of customer service and business operations. And they might be. But first, we need to talk about what happens when you give a robot unlimited authority and nobody's actually watching.
Why This Matters to You Right Now

If you're even casually exploring AI for your business — whether that's AI receptionists answering calls, chatbots handling customer questions, or anything else — you need to understand that these tools don't have instincts. They don't know when to stop. They don't think "hey, this is getting expensive." They just do what they're programmed to do, and if the guardrails aren't there, things can spiral fast.
An AI agent made nearly 5,000 calls in 96 hours without anyone noticing — in a company whose literal business is watching AI spending.

The scenario here was that the agent stayed open continuously, kept making calls, and kept incurring charges. It wasn't malicious. It wasn't hacked. It was just... nobody set spending limits or alerts. Nobody monitored it in real time. And by the time someone checked, the damage was done.
What You Actually Need to Do

items: Set hard spending caps BEFORE you deploy any AI agent — not after. Know your ceiling and enforce it automatically.
Get alerts set up so you know the moment your costs hit certain thresholds. Not daily reports. Alerts that ping you in real time.
Monitor actual usage for the first few weeks, not just costs. Are the calls making sense? Are they actually helping? Or is something weird happening?
Start small with AI agents. Test with a specific use case (like initial call screening) before you let it loose on your entire customer interaction funnel.
Have a kill switch ready. If something's off, you should be able to pause or shut down the agent immediately without losing data.

content.label: Intecha's Take
content.text: AI agents are genuinely useful — but they need guardrails the same way your employees need budgets. You wouldn't give someone unlimited authority to make business decisions without oversight, and you shouldn't do it with AI either. Start conservative, monitor closely, and scale up only when you're confident in what's actually happening.
